item.title: Reproducible Builds: Reproducible Builds in October 2026
item.author: Reproducible Builds
item.content:encoded: In our reports, we try to outline the most important things that we have been up to over the past month. As a quick recap about what problem our project intends to solve, whilst anyone may inspect the source code of free software for malicious flaws, almost all software is distributed to end users as pre-compiled binaries. The motivation behind the reproducible builds effort is to ensure no flaws have been introduced during this compilation process by promising identical results are always generated from a given source, thus allowing multiple third parties to come to a consensus on whether a build was compromised or not.As ever, if you are interested in contributing to the project, please visit our page on our website.In this month’s report, we cover:GNU ‘sparse archive’ non-determinism reportedJohannes Schauer Marin Rodrigues () reported an issue to the GNU mailing list where creating PAX-format sparse tar archives produces unreproducible outputs. Specifically, when GNU generates a PAX archive containing a sparse file it embeds the process ID into the member filename path structure (e.g. ./GNUSparseFile.<pid>/<filename>). Because process IDs vary between build runs, however, archiving identical sparse input files yields different binary outputs.In his report, Johannes outlined potential workarounds, such as running inside an unshared PID namespace where the process ID is pinned to , and proposed that GNU either omit the PID by default or provide a command-line flag to suppress it. Full details can be found in the post itself, and Johannes also filed the bug in Debian for completeness.Reproducible Builds at SeaGL 2026Reproducible Builds was present at SeaGL in Seattle, WA, on October 23rd & 24th. Thanks to everyone who attended and spoke with us!Members of the Reproducible Builds project attended SeaGL (the Seattle GNU/Linux Conference) in Seattle, WA, on October 23rd & 24th. It was a fantastic opportunity to connect with local community members, discuss software supply chain security and share updates on build verification tooling. Thanks to everyone who stopped by our sessions or spoke with us during the event.Founded in 2013, SeaGL is an annual free-as-in-freedom, grassroots technical summit dedicated to spreading awareness, community engagement and practical knowledge about free software, open hardware and libre culture. is our in-depth and content-aware diff utility that can locate and diagnose reproducibility issues. This month, Chris Lamb made a number of changes, including preparing and uploading versions , , and to Debian:Support the binary being called on the host/runtime system. […]Drop from the package as it is not minimal. (#1114739) […]Fix a crash when using the latest version(s) of Androguard. Thanks, hc! […]Re-order various parts of the file comparator to make it easier to progressively delve into its functionality. […]Fix a silly “prepend” typo. […]Reflect in the Python packaging that the use of the language feature necessarily requires Python 3.10+. […]Update . […]Update copyright years. […]In Debian this month, 20 reviews of Debian packages were added, 28 were updated and 27 were removed this month adding to our knowledge about identified issues. One issue type was updated to reflect that Debhelper ‘’ level 14 is no longer experimental. […] specification updatesBernhard’s proposed modifications were independent of one another, allowing for any combination to be merged depending on community feedback. Bernhard noted that one proposal may see the most debate, and could still benefit from further refinement before reaching consensus. Community members are invited to review and provide feedback on the individual merge requests; as Bernhard writes, “The other MRs could still use feedback from more people before December”. Input can be submitted via reactions or comments on Salsa, directly by email to Bernhard or the mailing list.The specification was first published in 2015 and updated in 2017.The Reproducible Builds project detects, dissects and attempts to fix as many currently-unreproducible packages as possible. We endeavour to send all of our patches upstream where applicable or possible. item.title: Steinar H. Gunderson: Solving the fox game
item.author: Steinar H. Gunderson
item.content:encoded: Christoffer Stjernlöf posted about the Fox Game, an old Norse asymmetric board game (seemingly also called “halatafl”) where twenty sheep try to outsmart two foxes and get to the other side. His AI uncovered some interesting insights, but left the question open as of whether the foxes or the sheep actually win with perfect play (the general sentiment in his family was that winning with the foxes was easy). This was too tempting for me to leave on the table, so I set out to make a strong solve.Since I don't know this game myself, I've stayed with the rules he describes even when they differ from e.g. Wikipedia (in particular, I do not use forced fox jumps, or multi-jumps); the only real change is that I don't have a 40-move draw rule, any position that is a forced win for one of the sides would be a win no matter how long it would take. (I consider this just an implementation detail in his AI, although morally, I consider a draw a loss for the sheep.) You might want to read his post to get the full rules, because I'm not going to repeat them here.The results first: The sheep win with perfect play, even with only 19 sheep (remove one on the flank), or 18 if they are allowed to go first. Even with only 9 sheep (the minimum possible that isn't an instant win for the foxes), the sheep can force a draw right from the start. With one fox, 11 sheep suffice for a forced win. (The draw margin is seemingly so large because one fox can just camp in the last spot in the pen, and it's hard to force it away without getting harassed by the other fox, unless you have lots of sheep.)The rest is about the implementation. I'll skip over a lot of wrong turns, and unsurprisingly, there were a lot of bugs to iron out, but hopefully, it got to a good place in the end. :-) I started out trying to make something very simple, and it worked for the first few cases, but then things got more complicated than I would have liked in the end. Still only at ~1000 lines of code, though, with no dependencies.The board has 33 squares. I tried a few different ways of represent the state of the game, and ended up on a simple bitboard representation: There's a 64-bit bitmap representing where there are sheep, and another bitmap representing where there are foxes. Since there's plenty of room in there, I use a spare bit to represent side-to-move. This is compact (which mattered a lot earlier on, but not as much later), easy to iterate over, and has little redundancy, so it's easy to keep valid. You need fast 64-bit population count and bit-scan instructions, but a) that's common now everywhere, and b) I decided fairly early that I wanted to require BMI2 anyway.The bit order mostly doesn't matter; I just started at top-left and went from there. All it really influences is square iteration order. There's a small tweak in that I store the right half of the board mirrored (reverse x order) for symmetry purposes; more on that below.I just typed in every possible move from every square into an array, then verified by generating some SVGs that I hadn't made any typos (I had). In retrospect, I should have done something more automated; it would have been less painful.The moves for sheep are just “you can go to X, Y or Z”. The moves for foxes are “you can go to X or Y, or you can go to Z if there's a sheep at W (which will be eaten)”. The move generator mostly just looks up the source square and tests every move. For the sheep, I make an easy test using bitboards; for the foxes, I could probably do something similar, but the jump moves proved a bit tricky (even with PEXT/PDEP) and I didn't end up using it.This is the part that really determines the geometry of the board (apart from debugging display). Everything else is pretty much geometry-agnostic.There's a little over 2^41 possible board states (this includes some illegal positions as well as some situations that could never arise during actual gameplay, such as a fox being stuck at C1 with a row of sheep ahead of it), and I want to remember all of them. With that many positions, I figured I needed a fairly compact representation. I needed to store that a position could be sheep win, fox win or a draw, and then there was a fourth “invalid” state that was useful for internal reasons, so that maps exactly to two bits per position. (A tablebase intended for distribution could be compressed to less using the usual tricks of entropy coding, skipping half of the positions, or similar.)This means we need to give a number to every possible position, ideally one with no collisions and no holes. I learned about combinatorial number systems which fit the bill exactly; given e.g. “we have 33 squares and 15 pieces”, it gives a dense mapping of positions from board to ID (ranking) and the opposite (unranking). (I made some fairly fast ranking and unranking algorithms, which may or may not have been novel, but it turned out I didn't actually need fast unranking after some other optimizations.) There are some extra complications in that there are two types of pieces, but you can solve them in a number of ways.On a macro level, I store everything with 9 sheep and 1 fox first, then 9 sheep and 2 foxes, 10 sheep and 1 fox, and so on. This gives beautiful locality (a single move can never remove more than one sheep, and only extremely rarely more than one fox), allowing me to just mmap everything and let the kernel deal with it, even though I only had 256GB of RAM and the total set was larger (329,870,110,455 bytes after the symmetry optimizations below).mmap is almost never the right answer, but again, I was trying to go for simplicity. It certainly brought me pain, though, and perhaps some more explicit I/O would have been better.The board is left-right symmetric (with an odd number of columns, so that there is a middle column that is neither “left” nor “right”). I had hoped to just ignore this, but eventually the gains became too important to ignore, so I conceded.The basic idea is that I ranked the board twice, both as itself and mirrored (mirroring is just a couple of masks and shifts, given my representation), and picked the key that was the smaller as canonical. This reduced the number of positions I needed to look at to a bit over 50%, as expected, but it does nothing to the storage/RAM requirements; the new rank is not dense and the “illegal” (non-canonical) positions are spread out a bit all over the place (although of course near the low and high ends of values, it works much better).As a tweak, I chose to compute all 33+281 canonical fox positions and renumbered using those placements as an assumption. This slashes ~95% of the waste, which is good enough; you can still rank a nonconical position if the foxes are symmetric about the center (or if there's only one fox and it's in the middle!), though.You can improve on this by making the macro-splitting finer; instead of having a chunk for e.g. “10 sheep, 2 foxes”, you could have one with “5 sheep in left, 0 foxes in left, 1 sheep center, 1 fox center, 4 sheep in right, 1 fox in right” and demand that there are more sheep in left than right. However, you still get problems when the number is balanced, you'd need finer splitting etc.. The gains are small enough that I didn't see the point in doing this, and it tends to be a place where it's easy to introduce bugs.I imagined calculating the exact number of positions up to symmetry would be an interesting exercise somehow, but I suppose it just immediately falls to Burnside's lemma as soon as you know how to count positions at all.Now that we have positions and moves and a way to store results, we want to know how to find the result for the starting position (and ideally also all other positions).My first attempt just did a depth-first search, caching as it went. This worked for the earlier stages but was generally a disaster; it ran out of stack easily (even with 8 GB—eight of stack), and had problems with figuring out loops. (It didn't loop infinitely, but was prone to declaring loops where one side could break out of the loop by winning. I had a nasty hack to fix that, but it didn't really feel good.)What I did instead was propagating results one step at a time. For each possible position:If from a given position you know you can immediately win (e.g., the sheep reach the pen, or the fox eats the last relevant sheep), mark it as such.If you can, in one move, reach a known-won position, mark your position as won (for the side to move). Similarly, if you can only reach known-lost positions, mark your position as lost.Repeat #2 over and over again until you no longer have changes.This was simple but still inefficient; I typically needed 40–80 passes for each chunk (where a chunk is something like “all positions with 15 sheep, 2 foxes”). However, it was super-easy to parallelize; I have 64 cores and could just hand out reasonable independent sub-chunks, you don't even need locking or atomic operations on the result set.The correct way of doing this is retrograde analysis (replace #2 with doing backwards moves) and I assume this would have made the calculation roughly ten times as fast. But I only needed ~36 hours for the actual run (plus numerous pre-runs that failed for various reasons!), so I never got to this. After all, I wanted something simple to begin with.Since I only store win/draw/loss (WDL) for each position (also known as a “bitbase” in chess tablebases), it's not easy to know what the way to win is; just that “this move does not mess it up, the other side still can't force a draw”. However, in practice, you could just do reasonable-looking moves that don't regress the position, and take forward moves whenever you can (i.e., do sheep pushes if that still wins).I made a simple alpha-beta searcher that tries to get win distances using the bitbase as a guide, which was a really fun challenge! It can find wins when they're perhaps ~20 ply (10 moves for each side) away, depending a bit on how narrow the win is (if there are only a few ways to win, it will obviously have to search a much smaller tree). Ultimately, though, alpha-beta for finding exact mate scores is just a losing game, since even perfect move ordering will only give you a sqrt() improvement over pure minimax.Perhaps making DTZ (distance-to-zeroing, referring to zeroing the draw move counter in e.g. chess) bases would be possible without breaking the bank on storage space; I would assume that usually, you can force some sort of progress pretty fast, at least as the sheep.I made a very rudimentary interface to the database; the UI isn't very nice, and it largely relies on hovering (which doesn't work all that well on mobile) but I didn't want a polished game-player, just to know the answer. :-) You can try it out at https://sheep.sesse.net/, although I don't envision keeping it up forever. Perhaps someone can gain new insight from it and become an expert player, although strong solves are rarely very insightful in themselves due to the brute-force nature. At least we've conclusively settled (again, under this ruleset!) that the sheep win with perfect play.Earlier, I would publish the source, but these days, the only ones who would be reading it would be the AI beast (fox?), and I'm not really so interested in that. :-) I'm definitely open to answering questions if anyone should have them; contact information at my home page as usual.

item.title: Amin Bandali: Building GNU Emacs from source
item.author: Amin Bandali
item.content:encoded:
In the recent years, I've been configuring and building GNU Emacs from source, specifically the branch of the repository. Doing so allows me to use and test latest Emacs features, test my Emacs Lisp code with the laest developments in Emacs, and easily contribute my own changes to Emacs.Before we start, I recommend reading the file in the Emacs source repository for building Emacs from source tarballs, and also for details about building Emacs from its source repository. The information provided here were built upon the details documented in those files. When in doubt, consult those files as the main, authoritative source of information for how to build Emacs from source.Installing build dependenciesTo build GNU Emacs from its source repository, we first need to install the various required tools and build dependencies of Emacs. On Debian-based systems, this can be done using . First, we need to add the source packages for the current release of our Debian-based distribution in apt's configuration by adding the corresponding deb-src lines in an apt source list file. For currently existing and older Debian releases, that would be done by adding a corresponding deb-src line for each deb line in , such as:deb http://deb.debian.org/debian/ trixie main deb-src http://deb.debian.org/debian/ trixie main In systems with recent apt versions with so-called modernized sources that might look editing a file like /etc/apt/sources.list.d/debian.sources and adding deb-src to the Types lines:Types: deb deb-src URIs: http://deb.debian.org/debian/ Suites: trixie Components: main Signed-By: /usr/share/keyrings/debian-archive-keyring.gpg Then run to have apt download package information from the configured sources.We can now run to have apt download and install the build dependencies of Emacs. Debian-based distributions have packages for a few different configurations of Emacs, like with PGTK support for Wayland, and for Emacs without GUI support, which we can use with apt build-dep to download the specific dependencies of those configurations.Cloning the Emacs source repositoryAfter installing Git using if not already installed, we're now ready to clone the Emacs source repository from GNU Savannah:git clone https://https.git.savannah.gnu.org/git/emacs.git We can add to make a shallow clone of the repository, if we don't care about having a complete log of previous commits to the Emacs repository (shallow clones are much faster).If cloning over HTTPS is slow, we can try cloning over Git's own protocol (with the caveat that the repository is cloned over an insecure channel) or over SSH if we have a Savannah account, using one of the following URLs instead of the one above:
git://git.git.savannah.gnu.org/emacs.git ssh://git.savannah.gnu.org/srv/git/emacs.git Configuring the Emacs buildWe now change to the Emacs repository directory we just cloned, and run the script once to generate the script, which we will use to configure Emacs to our liking:To configure Emacs, the simplest approach is to run without any additional options, to have it use the defaults. We can get a list of available configuration options by running:As I rebuild Emacs frequently, I normally don't "install" it, but for a typical setup, we'll want to specify the installation directory using , e.g.:./configure --prefix=$HOME/.local Later, will install Emacs under the specified directory.By default, some of the files (such as ) will be compressed during installation. We can prevent that using --without-compress-install.For my builds, I always use these configuration options:--without-gconf --without-gsettings --without-gpm --with-native-compilation As I don't use the GNOME desktop, the GConf and GSettings integrations are always more trouble than useful for me, so I disable them. Further, I disable the GPM support, since I never use the mouse when using Emacs in the terminal. Lastly, I explicitly enable native compilation support.In Wayland environments, I usually use PGTK:And in X11 environments (e.g. EXWM), I either use the Lucid toolkit:--with-x-toolkit=lucid --with-xaw3d --with-x-toolkit=no --without-xaw3d Later after building Emacs, we can view the configuration options in Emacs by inspecting the system-configuration-options variable.After running , we can now finally build Emacs by running . The first build will take a while, since all of Emacs is being built from scratch. Subsequent builds will generally be faster.We can optionally run to install Emacs into the specified earlier, or the default . Note that this step might require using if our user doesn't have write permission for the .After building Emacs, we run it either from the install location if we ran earlier, or directly from the source repository. Currently, Emacs's build system makes a symlink to the latest built binary in the repository at , and for and other auxiliary binaries under the directory.When skipping , we might still want to be able to easily launch Emacs from anywhere by typing . We can do that by making symlinks to and its auxiliary binaries inside a directory in our , such as , like so:cd $HOME/.local/bin ln -s $HOME/src/emacs/src/emacs . for e in \ ebrowse emacsclient etags make-docfile\ make-fingerprint hexl rcs2log; do\ ln -s $HOME/src/emacs/lib-src/$e .; done For non-install setups like this, I augment in my init file with the location of the info manuals in the repository to make them known to Emacs:(defvar Info-directory-list) (with-eval-after-load 'info (setq Info-directory-list `(,@Info-directory-list ,(expand-file-name (convert-standard-filename "info/") source-directory) "/usr/share/info/"))) We can pull in the latest changes in the Emacs repository using , then rebuild our Emacs by running .Occasionally, rebuilds may fail due to bad interaction of changes with leftover build artifacts. In such cases, the easiest thing to do would be a for an almost-from-scratch build. On even rarer occasions, might also fail. We would then want to run to remove every file that's not tracked by Git, as if we freshly cloned the repository. In such cases, we would need to configure the build again using and provide the desired options before running again.Protesilaos's similar post from early 2025 was part of the inspiration for writing and sharing my version:https://protesilaos.com/codelog/2025-03-22-emacs-build-source-debian/Lastly, to reiterate, Emacs's own and files for building from source:Take care, and so long for now.

item.title: Freexian Collaborators: Debian Contributions: Python 3.15 transition, OpenSSH GSS-API package split improvements and more! (by Anupa Ann Joseph)
item.author: Anupa Ann Joseph
item.content:encoded: Python 3.15 transition, by Stefano Rivera with a little help from Colin WatsonDebian has started the transition to add Python 3.15 as a supported version alongside 3.14, which is still the default version. Stefano uploaded Python 3.15.0 final to unstable.Maximiliano Curia has been test-rebuilding the archive in Debusine with Python 3.15 as a supported version and prepared some patches to dh-python to smooth over some common failure points. Stefano reviewed these MRs, applying some and implementing alternative approaches for some of the issues.Debian only has multiple supported Python versions during the transition to a new version, and typically this shows up some bugs in packages. This time was no different, the common failure was many packages that installed intermediate build artifacts into the Python module tree. Some of these artifacts would differ between Python versions. We decided to detect both of these and fail the package build, rather than silently ship garbage in the binary packages. Colin helped to fix quite a bit of the build fallout from this.OpenSSH GSS-API package split improvements, by Colin WatsonThe recent GSS-API package split has largely gone relatively smoothly, but there was a subtle problem for people switching from one variant to the other: installing the replacement packages followed by purging the old one would cause some configuration files to disappear. Colin fixed this, and also reviewed and merged some autopkgtest contributions from Andreas Hasenack to make sure that this doesn’t regress in future.Miscellaneous contributionsCarles, using check-relations, investigated and reported 52 bugs for packages which have Recommended packages that are not available in Debian anymore. Followed up bugs on the topic.Carles added support to check-relations to detect Recommends that recommend a transitional package.Carles submitted merge requests (MR89, MR90, MR91, MR92) to the Debian developers-reference to remove or update references to packages that are not available anymore, have their name changed, have typos, etc.Carles investigated and opened bugs regarding notifications on LXDE (#1151954, #1151955) and added a section related to notifications on the Wiki.Helmut released asyncvarlink/0.3.3 to fix several bugs including connection robustness fixes by Alex Kiernan. Colin uploaded it to Debian.Helmut uploaded guess-concurrency to improve behavior on riscv64 by taking swap into account thanks to Adrian Bunk and Aurelien Jarno.Helmut sent patches for 55 cross build failures.Emilio updated some X11 libraries that fixed security vulnerabilities.Emilio managed various transitions.Raphaël updated gnome-shell-extension-hamster to work with GNOME 51 that was uploaded to Debian unstable.Stefano backported postsrsd 2.4.1 to Debian trixie.Stefano installed security updates on debian.social infrastructure.October saw a series of security releases for Python, due to the eMudhra key compromise incident. Stefano uploaded cPython 3.15.2, 3.14.10, and 3.13.18 which include blocks for the compromised intermediate CAs.Stefano reviewed CVEs fixed in recent cPython releases.Stefano uploaded PyPy3 8.0.1 to unstable.Stefano reviewed some of the wafer-debconf MRs that came in as part of Antonio’s Outreachy project.Stefano uploaded python-authlib, with security updates. And started preparing a stable update with backports of these patches.Stefano looked at the latest upstream version of munkres and submitted some 32-bit test failure fixes upstream. A new upstream maintainer has been very busy building out accelerated versions of the algorithms with AI assistance.Thorsten was finally able to fix the autopkgtest of cups. Afterwards he uploaded the latest version of cups to unstable.Santiago proposed a merge request for the Salsa CI pipeline to fix how logs were stored in the piuparts job.Lucas reviewed and merged community contributions to Ruby 3.4 in Debian unstable.Lucas coordinated with the security team and fixed multiple CVEs reported against Ruby 3.3 in Debian stable.Colin did quite a bit of work on the Python 3.15 transition, fixing lots of build and test fallout.Colin upgraded python-maturin from 1.9.4 to 1.16.0, helping with several Rust transitions; this involved more or less completely reworking our patch stack.Colin improved the packaging of the Frescobaldi frontend to LilyPond to help with his amateur music typesetting work, fixing its missing desktop entry, icon, and translations based on a patch set by Joachim Wiedorn.Anupa joined the Publicity team meeting to discuss upcoming events and activities of the Debian Publicity Team including on-boarding meeting for new contributors.Antonio spent quite some time welcoming Outreachy applicants to the DebConf/MiniDebConf websites project, replying to questions, reviewing contributions, etc. One of them will be selected for an internship that will start in December.Antonio spent some time investigating problems with Salsa background job processing, leading to an upstream bug report.

item.content:encoded: My Debian contributions this month were all sponsored by Freexian.Other build/test failures:Since lots of Python modules use Rust extensions nowadays, we often have to help with upgrades of Rust packages. It was already packaged in Debian, but it had a missing desktop entry and icon and missing translations; I fixed those based on a patch set by Joachim Wiedorn. My upload introduced a testing migration problem, which I also fixed.I upgraded rust-jiter and rust-smallvec to new upstream versions for a new version of pydantic-core. The rust-smallvec upgrade caused an in rust-saphyr-parser-bw, which I fixed.I improved the tool used by the Rust team to check build-depends too, which should make it easier for that team to remember Python packages in transitions.

item.title: Russell Coker: Thinkpad T14
item.author: etbe
item.content:encoded: It has been working reasonably well for me, but my vision is diminishing so my current setup with the Kitty terminal emulator allows 4 terminals of 153/154 columns and 40/41 rows or 9 terminals of about 101*27. To have this much text I use the minimum font size I can see which is unreadable when I first wake up – which is bad for the “woken by network management system alert” situations. Also 16G of RAM is a bit of a limit, the Thinkpad X1 Carbon has 4G of swap space and it’s all used most of the time. While there’s usually plenty of buffer/cache RAM it does sometimes get to an OOM situation.Another issue is that the battery is approaching it’s end of life. The “” command reports the following which might imply that the battery should last more than 80% of the time when it was new, but testing shows that the time I can use it on battery is not much more than half what it was when I bought the laptop, maybe 1/3 of the battery life when new. I used to be able to consistently run the machine on battery for 7+ hours and still have plenty of charge left, now I can’t even get 5 hours.energy-full: 50.35 Wh energy-full-design: 57.02 WhI could buy a new battery for about $70, but there are plenty of things I can do with that laptop for which 1/3 the designed battery life is more than enough. Also I have a couple of USB-C batteries that are capable of supplying 30W+ to power a Thinkpad X1 Carbon but they are inconvenient and I’d rather have external batteries and an internal battery that will last most of a day.Below is a table summarising most of the Thinkpads I’ve owned. I really like the Trackpoint on Thinkpads and have not considered buying a laptop without one. I skipped two laptops I bought in the 2000-2002 time period, that was an expensive laptop time for me. Fortunately by 2000 ebay was getting useful so I only ever had to buy one brand new Thinkpad.weight screen resolution CPU and RAMoverheating and screen backlightoverheating battery-life and PSUlid hinge broken and generally olderror on proprietary SSD lack of USB-C and screen resolutionscreen resolution and wanted a 2in1RAM and screen resolutionSo I’ve spent $2675.70 on Thinkpads that I used from 2010 until now (not counting the one I just bought), so that’s $160 per annum for the past 16 years and 9 months.When I convert that to 2025/2026 dollars that’s $3,221 for 16 years 9 months or $198 per annum. So I just need to make this T14 last for 2 years to be spending less than usual.Some Generic Laptop AdviceA while ago I was asked for advice on buying a laptop for an architect to use. I can give good advice for laptops used by programmers and for home use and students but I really don’t know what an architect does and even a description wouldn’t do it justice.The advice I gave was to buy or borrow a relatively low end laptop, something that costs $400 new or $300 second hand and give it a go. Using it will reveal that it doesn’t do what is desired in some ways, whether it’s screen resolution, RAM, CPU power, storage capacity, physical size/weight, or some combination of them is something you won’t know until you try it. Then after having used a cheap laptop they could buy a laptop for $1500+ (for serious work use by people outside the IT industry buying a new laptop is recommended) knowing what features they really need.So I have gone through a similar process of buying different laptops and discovering the benefits which has arrived at the T14.I saw a Thinkpad T14 with 4K display and 16G of RAM on Facebook Marketplace advertised for $400 and they ended up selling it to me for $300 without the SSD and without the PSU. The seller has a business of selling used enterprise gear so he was happy to keep the SSD and PSU for sale with other laptops. I don’t have a need for more laptop PSUs as I have most of the laptops in my fleet charged from 200W+ PSUs that charge multiple devices and I also have a collection of spare SSDs.$300 for a laptop with 4K display is a good deal. The T14 is significantly better than the T14s because it has one SODIMM socket while the T14s has soldered RAM, so I could expand the RAM to 48G at some future time – but with current prices I bought an 8G SODIMM for $40 so 24G will have to do for now. That gives a total of $340 plus the value of a SSD.My first tests with the 4K display I set the display scaling to 150% (previously I had 100% which was a little small for some parts of the display). For my current favourite terminal emulator Kitty I had the Terminus font set to 10.5 point and now have it set to 9.0 point. This set of changes took the amount of text displayed in terminals from about 300*80 to about 330*100 while also increasing readability. This is a very significant improvement. If I knew that 4K in a 14″ display would be so good I’d have got it years ago!The i7-10610U in my new Thinkpad scores only about 10% faster on Passmark than the i7-8550U in my previous one. That’s disappointing given that Intel had another 3 years of research to develop it and it’s running with faster RAM. The two CPUs have the same TDP so it’s just a 10% performance gain over 3 years and no change anywhere else. If the new CPU had a lower TDP then the small performance increase would be understandable.When I first booted the system Chrome graphics were corrupted and system performance was bad, after installing the packages and to deal with the kernel errors about not finding firmware the graphics display was correct and the system ran a lot faster. I had forgotten about the issues related to having NVidia and Intel GPUs on the same system that I had dealt with in previous T series Thinkpads.In the systemd-boot loader.conf file I added “console-mode 0” to prevent the font being ridiculously small for the boot selection.The battery life seems like it might be a bit less than my previous laptop was when I got it, but it’s definitely better than the previous laptop gives now.The screen is very shiny, I prefer the screens with matt finish to avoid seeing reflections. The “anti glare” screens for the T14 are for FullHD and worse while the “glossy” screen is the only option for 4K.. Maybe I should investigate one of those hoodie jackets with a hood that’s large enough to cover the screen, they are being sold as a privacy feature but can also be used to avoid reflection. As an aside if you are in an environment with hostile parties then you really shouldn’t block your vision of them.A problem I previously had with T series Thinkpads which contributed to the replacement of two of them is the screen hinges breaking. This laptop is significantly heavier and more solidly built than the X1 series I’ve been using and opening and closing the screen takes a lot more force. I am now wondering if I’ll be looking for a “for parts” condition Thinkpad on ebay in the future. It seems that cracking the screen is a much more common failure case than breaking the hinges so hopefully there will be spares available. But as my previous T series thinkpads lasted 7, 3, and 4 years this one could be expected to last until 2030 and maybe by then giving it to someone in Vietnam and buying a replacement would be the easiest option.I thought that going from 2560*1440 to 3840*2160 I would be hitting the diminishing returns range but it seems that there are still further gains to be found in screen resolution for my use, maybe the Apple people with their “Retina” displays are on to something. There are Thinkpad X1 Carbon models with 3840*2400 displays, so maybe that’s something to move on to in a few years. The minimum model with 3840*2400 is the X1 Carbon Gen 9 and there’s the X1 Yoga Gen 6 with an OLED 3840*2400. There’s also the P series which has 16″ 3840*2400 displays which would allow more usable text with the caveat of being much less portable.It sucks that no-one seems to be making a laptop with more than 3840*2400 resolution. 5120*2160 desktop monitors are common and affordable nowadays. I’m sure that even now I could use more than 3840*2400 in a 14″ laptop and when I was younger I could have benefited from more than 3840*2400 in an 11″ laptop if such hardware had been available.

item.title: Louis-Philippe Véronneau: A good-looking Corsi-Rosenthal Box
item.author: Louis-Philippe Véronneau
item.content:encoded: Ever since I built an AirGradient boardback in 2023, I have been more and more conscientious about air quality. Pretty instantly after installing the board in my living room, I realised common habits like cooking can significantly increase the particulate levels in my entire apartment.Here is a good example of a pretty large (and long-lasting) PM spike on September 23 after cooking a meal:Isn't this crazy? Last time Montreal had such bad outdoor air quality, there were public broadcasts telling people not to go outside and to wear N95 face masks if we absolutely needed to. Inside my apartment though, no one ever told me cooking veggies in a little oil on medium-low could make the air I breathe unsafe.This of course is aggravated by the fact my apartment is pretty much as airtight as it can reasonably be, since winters here are very cold and air infiltrations are a major heat loss source. As such "opening my windows when I cook" is not a viable solution to this problem half of the year.I first tried solving this issue by tuning my HVAC system. Sadly, its controls don't offer much flexibility, which means it is not the right tool to respond to short-lived spikes like these. Not only this, but the quality of the air outside is not always good either: Canada now has a forest fire season (we're all doomed) and my neighbors regularly smoke cigarettes right under my HVAC air intake.Clearly, the solution to this particular issue was to buy an air purifier. Or at least, that's what a "normal" people would have done. Sadly, these units are expensive, use (expensive) proprietary filters, don't work very well and can be loud.One of the great inventions of the COVID-19 pandemic is the Corsi-Rosenthal box. Popularised in 2020 by Richard Corsi and Jim Rosenthal, the idea is to make a DIY air purifier by using a large fan to force air through cheap and readily available MERV13 air filters.The main downsides of regular CR boxes is they are pretty ugly, can be loud depending on the fan used and need to be rebuilt when the filters are changed (they are held using tape).That's when I stumbled on this amazing design for a silent and sleek CR box sold by The 3D Handyman. Clearly, with a bit of tinkering and a 3D printer, I could also design something sleek, silent and efficient!Since I was already using MERV13 air filters in my HVAC, I decided to design around 4 vertical "beams" where the filters would slot in. With tight enough tolerances, I figured I could get rid of the complex moving parts in The 3D Handyman's design. I also added M5 threads to screw the top and bottom panels and the TPU feet to elevate the box from the floor.The final result looks like this. I used some foamcore boards I had laying around at work for the top and bottom panels, but any somewhat rigid plastic panels (like coroplast) would also work: out' position" alt="The whole CR box assembled, with the fan in the 'in -> out' position">I ended up having to split the "beams" in two and joining them with dowels, as even the largest 3D printers I had access to couldn't print them in one piece.Here's the cost breakdown for this project (shipping and taxes are included):The fan is . It is by far the best fan I have ever owned. Not only it is all metal and very quiet, but it is also PWM-controlled via a USB-C controller, which means the speed it runs at can be automated. I have been using it constantly and take it out of the CR box during the summer to be used as a "regular" fan. I like it so much so I am seriously considering buying the 14 inch model.The 3D printed parts are plastic and they will last me a lifetime.As mentioned before, the filters are the same I use in HVAC, which means I can buy them in packs of 12 to reduce costs.All in all, I'm very happy with this project. Since finishing it, I have been able to consistently get the PM levels in my apartment down to zero and significantly reduce the time it takes to recover from a spike caused by cooking food.I certainly could have cut the cost of this project in half by choosing a cheaper fan, like the box fans used in the reference Corsi-Rosenthal instructions, but I decided to spend more for a more quiet and reliable option.Here are the STLs I used for this project. I certainly don't recommend just printing them as-is, since I am using the 12" x 12⅞" x ¾" custom air filters from my HVAC and you should probably use something more standard.If you use these files as inspiration, your goal should be to make a box that is 16" wide, to fit the AC Infinity fan comfortably. I printed the "beams" in PETG at 100% infill and the feet in TPU 95:The next step in this project is to automate the fan speed based on the PM levels in my apartment. At the moment, I manage this manually and it is becoming a chore.This should be relatively easy to do with a Raspberry Pi Pico board, since AC Infinity sells a USB-C to Molex adapter for the fan.

item.title: John Goerzen: The Large Project Bias of CVEs
item.author: John Goerzen
item.content:encoded: That turns out to be pretty difficult for a small independent project.Large projects have a way to self-assign CVE IDs. They are their own CVE Numbering Authority (CNA). There is a massive list of CNAs. Just looking at the first page of results, I see everyone from Airbus to 9front (the niche Plan 9 OS). The OpenKermit project is not a CNA.If you’re a CNA, you can create and publish CVEs on your schedule. There is apparently no external review process. You can wait for months, or publish immediately.If you’re not a CNA, you have to find someone that is. The general ones that are CNAs appear to be Github and MITRE.It’s been a week and a half and no sign of a review yet. Apparently the real review time is more than a month.The other option for projects without a CNA is via MITRE. You have to use a strange and often broken web form, logging in with either Google or Gitlab. (It seems to be broken on Firefox). Then you submit your request and wait.The first CVE I obtained for C-Kermit was CVE-2025-68920. At the time, I had not yet started the OpenKermit project. That issue was found and fixed in the context of my work maintaining C-Kermit for Debian, and Debian is a CNA.These were discovered while wearing my “upstream C-Kermit maintainer” hat. I’m sure I could ask Debian for CVEs again, but that seems a bit cheating; not everyone that maintains a FLOSS project will have connections with a distro like I do.There are a lot of components of a modern OS and Internet ecosystem that are small projects without a large institution behind them.This bias towards large organizations when it comes to communicating security problems benefits nobody. It doesn’t benefit users, and only serves to discourage timely communication. Not everyone is as persistent as I am, and when it is made so difficult to make announcements — which seem to go into a giant black hole — it’s easy to say, “why bother?”By Microsoft’s own admission, they are under-funding their CVE process on Github (which may also be poorly-designed). They blame it on increasing load due to LLMs — a problem they helped create and predicted! Having a fiction about being able to communicate a security issue in a reasonable time is worse than not offering the path at all.Linux was once a student’s experiment. Let’s not pretend that quality only matters from large projects.

item.title: Vasudev Kamath: Experiment: Debian Cloud/VM Images using mkosi
item.author: copyninja
item.content:encoded: Debian's Cloud Images for various public cloud platforms and VM environments are built using a tool called debian-cloud-images, an in-house utility developed and maintained by the .The tooling uses FAI (Fully Automatic Installation) to create custom VM images for public clouds like , , and , along with the class. I wanted to convert this into a fully declarative, mkosi-based image build where the entire image is described using INI-format configuration files, with only a few post-installation scripts to handle final customizations.I've been working with various image customization formats for a long time. In my previous company, I used to build customized industrial PC distributions based purely on Debian using and a bunch of shell scripts to stitch together raw image creation, bootloader installation, etc. I've also done custom installs using on my own laptop with as the bootloader, but that was mostly hand-crafted and not automated. Once I came across , I was impressed by how a single utility can do everything and churn out a fully usable image without extra glue scripts for partitioning and image creation. You still need a few scripts to finalize some parts of the installation (via postinst hooks), but those are very minimal.So I decided: why not convert into mkosi's declarative format with a few architectural changes? My requirements were:Btrfs as the root filesystem: Partly because I like it, but primarily for the ability to use transparent compression (), subvolumes, and snapshots for atomic rollbacks when things go wrong.systemd-boot and Unified Kernel Images (UKI): Primarily because is clean and minimal—exactly what a modern bootloader should be. Combining it with UKIs and UEFI Secure Boot is bliss compared to the complexity of the GRUB2 world.This intentionally drops legacy BIOS (MBR/CSM) partitioning support in favor of pure UEFI. Modern cloud platforms (AWS Nitro, Azure Gen2, GCP) support UEFI natively, and dropping BIOS allows shedding significant legacy bootloader baggage—though it does make these images unsuitable for older, non-UEFI hypervisors.Of course, the initial heavy lifting was done mostly using Antigravity (), along with debugging, tuning, and cleanup from my side. I pointed to a local copy of and laid out my requirements: preserve parity with the original packages and configurations, while enabling selective builds for each cloud via modular profiles. The resulting specification is documented here.The repository also includes a verification script that audits functional parity against official images produced by (verifying packages, APT deb822 sources, and systemd services, while accounting for the switch to Btrfs and systemd-boot). Initial verification was performed for all Trixie profiles, and the parity report is published here.I've also booted the profile image under UEFI in a local VM to verify live bootability, , network connectivity, and APT repository setup. This completes Phase 1 of the implementation. The remaining phases outlined in the specification include:Phase 2: Immutable Images with dm-verity: Configure in systemd-repart's . Enable mkosi auto-signing for the verity root hash and pass the root hash into UKI kernel command lines automatically.Phase 3: Secure Boot & Signed UKIs: Integrate with custom owner keys or using Microsoft Third-Party CA signed shim binaries.Phase 4: System Extensions (systemd-sysext): Decouple cloud vendor agents (AWS CLI, Azure waagent, GCP guest agent) into separate system extensions. Maintain a single unified, signed base OS image across all cloud platforms.Phase 5: Btrfs Automated Rollbacks: Combine Btrfs with systemd-boot snapshot boot entries for fail-safe OS upgrades.Another advantage of this setup is that the same tooling can build images for physical laptops and bare-metal servers. For example, in an earlier post, I walked through live-booting with and manually configuring for a custom UEFI installation. With , I can simply generate a customized image locally with UKIs ready to go, live-boot the target machine, and write the image directly to the root disk.This experiment is an exploration of the power of ; I haven't discussed adoption with the yet. For now, this will continue as my pet project. While I won't be hosting pre-built binary images, anyone interested is welcome to clone the repository and build the images locally.I will probably take some more time before tackling dm-verity images, as I want to understand the nuances thoroughly before experimenting with them. Until then, happy hacking! Please report any issues or suggestions on GitHub.

item.title: Amin Bandali: EmacsConf 2026 community panel - my comments
item.author: Amin Bandali
item.content:encoded: This is a recollection of my comments from the EmacsConf 2026 community panel recording session this past weekend, where the panellists took turns answering the proposed questions, one minute per question per panellist.In addition to the live Q&A session planned for Saturday 12 December 2026 during EmacsConf 2026, all Emacs users and community members are invited to share their thoughts on the panel questions or other questions before or after the conference.1. What made you start using Emacs, and what kept you using it?I started using Emacs during my bachelor's studies. I actually learned about Vim first and was a Vim user, but I'd always found the configuration language (VimScript) a little bit clunky. Not long after, I discovered Emacs, and really loved reading and writing Emacs Lisp, so I stuck around.In addition to reading and writing Elisp being fun and enjoyable for me, I love that Emacs has been a practical embodiment of software freedom, and I'm really fond of its surrounding culture of sharing freely. There's a lot to love and appreciate about Emacs, but as a practical personal example, I've been grateful for its excellent support for bidirectional text editing. It has empowered me to read and write in Persian, my mother tongue, with ease. (Persian has a right-to-left alphabet, like Arabic and Hebrew.)2. What took you from using Emacs to actively contributing to the community - participating in forums, writing Elisp, organizing meetups, answering questions?As I continued experimenting and writing bits and pieces of Elisp to scratch my own itches, I felt compelled to share them freely as a way of giving back to the community that gave me so much.For me, the community and the people that make it up are the main deal. Emacs wouldn't be where it is and what it is today without its people, so besides programming contributions, I've tried to contribute in that area as well, for instance by reviving EmacsConf with Sacha Chua back in 2019.3. How does Emacs show up for you in real life - colleagues, meetups, friends? How did those connections form?I don't physically have people near me who use Emacs, but I've connected with many folks in our online communities, often starting with an email or IRC message. Some of those relationships started as acquaintanceship and were developed into true friendship over time, and I'm grateful to have had those friends with me.4. If you know other software communities, what's one thing Emacs could learn from them?I would encourage Emacs, our community, to focus on the people. We're living in particularly difficult times, with various kinds of hardships and uncertainty in our lives. Let's strive to treat each other with kindness, empathy, and mindfulness as we continue working together.There are great examples of other free software communities whose members have banded together and are strengthening each other and their community, as well as cautionary ones where community members have been tiring and driving out their fellow members. We could learn valuable lessons from both in how to take care of our people and ourselves.5. What's one concrete thing you wish existed in the Emacs community a year from now?I echoed the sentiments of my fellow panellists Prot and Til about doing more of the same in terms of continuing to uphold the standards of excellence and perseverance. Also, drawing inspiration from what bashbunni said, to lower the barriers of entry for people, for example through organizing different kinds of events, and experimenting with ways to make people's lengthy, elaborate Emacs configurations more tangible and accessible to others, to share various workflows and demonstrate what's possible with Emacs.I look forward to your thoughts on these and other community-related questions.Take care, and so long for now.

item.content:encoded: I ran the following benchmarks on an , a Zen 4c CPU, rented from Scaleway, running at 2.4 GHz with CPU boost disabled. I compiled the kernels with GCC 10.2: this version can compile older kernels as well as the current ones.Performance evolution of IPv6 route lookups. Versions with an asterisk have SRSO mitigation disabled.a recent full view with about 260,000 prefixes,a full view from 2017 with about 40,000 prefixes,a set of 40,000 /48 prefixes, such that 2 lookups out of 3 match, anda set of 40,000 random /128 prefixes, such that 1 lookup out of 400 matches.The major 200 ns regression introduced in Linux wiped out all these improvements. This version implements a mitigation for "Speculative Return Stack Overflow," a vulnerability affecting AMD processors, in commit fb3bd914b3ec. This mitigation adds about 20 cycles on each function return. It was backported to older kernels (5.10, 5.15, 6.1, and 6.4). To keep the results legible, I disabled the mitigation for these versions with on the kernel command-line.You can check the vulnerabilities impacting your CPU and their mitigations with . Some mitigations may depend on the microcode or on the firmware.lscpugrepPerformance evolution of IPv4 route lookups. Versions with an asterisk have SRSO mitigation disabled.I tested three scenarios:a recent full view with more than 1,000,000 prefixes,a subset of a full view from 2017 with 500,000 prefixes, anda set of 500,000 contiguous /32 prefixes.The 30 ns impact of the mitigation for in Linux is smaller than for IPv6 because IPv4 route lookups traverse fewer functions: around 4 function calls for IPv4 compared to 25 for IPv6.In Linux , I introduced a regression in commit c0c5a60f0f13 after fixing the behavior of net.ipv4.conf.all.ignore_routes_with_linkdown! item.content:encoded: For some time now I’ve been looking for a way of keeping projects I’m working on in a separate VM without much setup. There are numerous solutions to do this kind of thing using namespaces (various container technologies, firejail, flatpak, bubblewrap, …) but I wanted something that uses real virtualization. I recently stumbled upon incus and it seemed like it could be a solution to my problem. Incus is a manager for both containers and virtual machines. It is possible to create VM images that can be used as templates, meaning that other machines can then be based on them on creation. Virtual machines can be configured using “profiles”.For my use case, I have created a profile that defines how my template image should look like. In this profile I use cloud-init to configure the template machine on startup:and I use a script to regenerate the template image when I want to adapt the config:This script uses the image together with my profile to set up a machine, configure it using and store the result as an image called .To use this setup, I created a small python tool called inker that talks to the incus REST API. Using creates a new VM based on my template. Using attaches the current working directory to a VM as a readonly mount. It is possible to combine those commands like inker create | inker attach to do those two steps in one command. logs into the VM that has the current directory attached. This way I can create VMs that are connected to directories on my filesystem.I am currently playing around with this setup, but I think this could help me to have a throwaway development machine, similar to dev containers. I’m not sure yet how happy I am with , though. I was also looking at systemd-vmspawn, but there are still some features missing that I would need. But I might rewrite at some point to use a different backend.

item.title: Dirk Eddelbuettel: prrd 0.1.0 at CRAN: Now With Real Concurrency
item.author: Dirk Eddelbuettel
item.content:encoded: A new release of prrd arrived at CRAN today, and has already been built for r2u and on r-universe. The prrd package facilitates the parallel running [of] reverse dependency [checks] when preparing R packages. It is used extensively for releases I make of Rcpp, RcppArmadillo, RcppEigen, BH, and others.The key idea of prrd is simple, and described in some more detail on its webpage and its GitHub repo. Reverse dependency checks are an important part of package development that is easily done in a (serial) loop. But these checks are also generally as there is no or little interdependency between them (besides maybe shared build depedencies). See the (somewhat dated) screenshot (running six parallel workers, arranged in a split byobu session).This release updates internals to allow for greater concurrency. SQLite is used as the backend, both for the job queue (managed via the liteq package) as well as for storing actual reverse-dependency test results. It is well-known that SQLite copes quite well with multiple . Multiple concurrent are more challenging. We tended to get by via pragma use, but still get occassional issue even at a somewhat moderate concurrency levels. After some back and forth and trying a few approaches, more recently we established one first solution relying on very explicity (OS-level, filesystem-based) locking via package filelock. That worked.We mentioned this in an old issue that had circled around the same question with a number of posts over the years, but no resolution. This comment seemingly awoke Gábor, and he nailed this years-open issue with a fine pull request deploying and well as a loop around to not immediately fail. I borrowed/ported that approach to prrd and we now have a second solution (and no longer need filelock). On a somewhat better server with enough cores and memory, I am now running eighteen concurrent workers—watched via three multi-pane byobu windows. Works like a charm without issues. At last! A big thanks to Gábor for finding another solution, and especially that only relies on SQLite.The release is summarised in the NEWS entry:Changes in prrd version 0.1.0 (2026-11-07)Concurrent operations are now supported via updated sqlite semantics borrowed with appreciation from This follows an interim solution relying on use; however this later package is not needed so no increase in dependencies

item.title: Mike Gabriel: OpenAGPS - The New Kid on the Block
item.author: sunweaver
item.content:encoded: There is a new project coming to Open Source Software land these days: OpenAGPS. It is not yet 100% functional, but we are working on it. It is not fully operational, yet, but we are on it.Let me introduce OpenAGPS to you...The domain of assisted geo location services has been left to a few big tech providers. When using GPS on mobile devices, most of us send info on our approximate device location (based on cell tower IDs seen by our devices around us) mostly to Google's SUPL service in order to facilitate a faster GNSS/GPS lock on the satellites flying above us.Without assistance, retrieving a GNSS/GPS lock on sufficient satellites includes "finding" those satellites and once found retrieving data (in bytes/sec) from them. In some regions, this leads to waiting periods of up to 45 minutes, before a mobile devices has gained a lock on sufficient satellites (3 or more).In Assisted-GNSS/GPS, "other" information (such as cell tower IDs) gets used to estimate what GNSS/GPS satellites are currently passing over one's location. With AGPS, the mobile devices retrieve information via a so-called SUPL server, containing two details: a list of potential satellites above and their dataframes. Esp. providing those dataframes over the device's internet connection (and not via the GNSS/GPS receiver downloading it from the satellite itself) speeds up the lock-on process of the mobile tremendously (several seconds to a few minutes).However, for this mechanism to work, your device will share your IMSI (although not needed for AGPS), a list of cell towers around you and their signal strengths with the provider of the SUPL service, revealing your approximate position. In total, this allows SUPL providers to re-identify each mobile device and create motion profiles of each such device (and its owner). If the SUPL service is hosted by one main provider (i.e. Google SUPL), there is a lot of valuable information available to them for free that they can commercialize.Currently, there is only one mitigation method available to hide one's location info from the SUPL server(s) at e.g. Google: using a SUPL proxy server implementation (available as OSS, provided by and used in e.g. GrapheneOS). A SUPL proxy still depends on the big tech service provider(s) for SUPL as it merely proxies SUPL requests from mobile devices through to the proprietary SUPL services, at e.g. Google, but the mobile device is being camouflaged behind the SUPL proxy in use.OpenAGPS, on the contrary, will be a fully independent implementation from proprietary service providers, and it will refrain from collecting and commercializing end users’ data. It will be driven by individuals of the OpenAGPS community. There will likely be one central service that the OpenAGPS project plans to host and operate (the Porygon frontend/backend, OpenAGPS's GNSS Almanach service), but except from that SUPL servers can be self-hosted by individuals, companys or other communities. The requesting mobile devices' IDs will be hidden from the Porygon server (like with existing SUPL proxy implementations), so that the only centrally operated component (the Porygon Almanach server) does not know who is requesting what geo position information (and thus cannot collect such data, neither derive info about where requesting devices are located).In addition, with a large OpenAGPS community, it is imaginable (in theory) that there will also be multiple central Almanach servers available on the internet (with parallel networks of base stations attached to each GNSS Almanach server).Collecting Satellite DataThe OpenAGPS project is not simply a software that admins/users can install, it needs kind of a huge and global community to operate/host/house its base station network.The challenge with providing a community-driven AGPS service on the internet is that up-to-date (real-time!) GNSS/GPS satellite position data is not available for free download. Almanach data can be obtained per region from various organisations, but then their datasets are often days to weeks old, thus too outdated. GNSS/GPS satellites are not geo-stationary, they circulate around the planet. Their position is dependent on the current date-time. A globally spanning network of GNSS/GPS base stations will do the trick here. We will need a community that harvests the needed satellite data in real time and makes it available through the Porygon Almanach server to all OpenAGPS users.The OpenAGPS project will depend on at least one community member every ~40-50 km² to operate a so-called OpenAGPS base station: These base stations are stationary, need to run 24/7, and they will harvest GNSS/GPS statellite data information from the satellites above in real-time and share this data with the (central) Porygon server, continuously. The Porygon server will create a timestamp-dependent "map" of all seen satellites and extrapolate locations between base stations' Almanach data updates.Help making OpenAGPS a Success: Host a Base StationTo make OpenAGPS a success, we need volunteers who are willing to host (actually: house) an OpenAGPS base station at their home or work place (or both). Users will only be able to use their self-hosted OpenAGPS SUPL server with their mobile devices (instead of e.g. Google SUPL), if we manage to establish sufficient coverage with those base stations in the area of interest, so that the OpenAGPS Almanach will get populated with sufficient satellite position data.Support this project by Co-Funding itIf you realize that you have an interest in this project and would like to improve your level of digital sovereignty in your government, organization, at your home, etc. then consider sending financial support to the project. If you want to support us, please get in touch with Raoul Kramer at BetaBreak or Mike Gabriel at Fre(i)e Software GmbH. If you are a software developer and would like to contribute to OpenAGPS, also get in touch and let us meet at FOSDEM 2027.A huge thanks to the NLnet Foundation for funding this project's bootstrap phase. Follow-up funding has been applied for, so please keep fingers crossed!

item.title: Isoken Ibizugbe: Seeing Accessibility in Debian
item.author: Isoken Ibizugbe
item.content:encoded: Recently, I’ve been noticing something on packaging around my house that I used to glance right past: raised Braille dots on a carton of medicine, and embossed markings on a container of body cream. I’ve always known what Braille looked like, but I never paid close attention to it. Now that I’m actively working on accessibility testing for the Debian Installer, I see it everywhere.It made me reflect on how accessibility usually enters our consciousness. In tech, we’re taught about accessibility as a best practice when designing user interfaces or web apps. But realistically, you mostly see it implemented well in massive global software, like mobile operating systems or browsers like Firefox. You rarely see accessibility features integrated into local Nigerian physical products or everyday tech. Paying attention to these details made me realize how much care goes into making sure every person is considered, and how vital that mindset really is.Manual Testing & The openQA BottleneckMy recent work with Debian has been focused on automating tests for the Debian Installer’s accessibility features, specifically validating Braille display emulation.I started out by manually testing following the official steps on the Debian Installer Accessibility Wiki. Once I understood the manual flow, the next goal was figuring out how to automate it inside openQA.Initially, the idea was to initialize from the bootloader by adding parameters to the Grub (GRUB=”brltty=auto”)and it should start the installation with the braille visual. However, this didn’t work, the parameters never initiated the brttyl and it was a huge blocker going back and forth. Getting brltty to talk to the test runner in that environment would have required sweeping changes across the main Debian openQA instance configuration.Instead of pushing for complex system-wide changes on the instance, we started looking for easier alternative approaches and noted the complicated ones, when we advance in the test.We brainstormed streaming the display output directly to a dedicated file to capture and verify the Braille virtual display output. Ultimately, nested virtualization proved to be the most easiest path forward. You can check out the implementation details and changes in the Merge RequestAs part of this work, I joined the debian-accessibility mailing list to introduce what we were building and share our progress.The responses were encouraging. I got some feedback and suggestions and the thread also created a discussion on how accessible the installation process currently feels for blind or visually impaired users, and where they also find issues. It served as a great reminder that test suites aren’t just about passing CI checks, they’re about serving actual people who rely on these systems every day.

item.title: Vincent Bernat: Scriptable GeoDNS: leaving AWS for Bunny
item.author: Vincent Bernat
item.content:encoded: I disable logging to avoid collecting personal information. While the bunny.net GDPR page promises they anonymize data, it is unclear what CloudFront keeps in its own logs when logging is disabled.The only downside of the offering is the lack of HTTP/3. I asked their support: two minutes later, they answered they are working on it but have no to share.I run seven small NixOS virtual machines to host this blog around the world: Paris, Nuremberg, Ashburn, Singapore, San Jose, São Paulo, and Sydney. Bunny's scriptable DNS lets me return the IP addresses of the . The browser falls back to the second server if the first one is down.The above script relies on the RoutingEngine.getClosestServer() helper, which returns the closest alive server to the user. Thanks to Doggo, we can check it works as expected, at least for :doggo--gp-fromAvincent.bernat.ch doggo--gp-fromAvincent.bernat.ch The most annoying drawback of this method is that a user from Buenos Aires gets both São Paulo (1000 mi, 30 ms ) and Ashburn (5200 mi, 140 ms ). Most resolvers randomize the order, so the user may pull the web page from Ashburn. We could return only the nearest server—and swap the scripted record with the built-in geographic routing instead. But if the server becomes unavailable, the browser has no alternative until the DNS cache expires. It leaves a short window of unavailability, even with a short .The HTTPS record solutionThe HTTPS DNS record, defined in RFC 9460, solves both the availability and the latency issues. Modern browsers query this record to get additional information to reach an HTTP server, including an alternative port and the application layer protocol—HTTP/2 or HTTP/3. Each record has a priority. We can ask browsers to contact the nearest server first and fall back to the next one if the first is unavailable:This looks like the ideal solution! Unfortunately, Chrome ignores any record whose target is not , hence the last record at priority 3. Moreover, unlike with a , Bunny DNS does not return the IP addresses for and in the additional section. The resolver needs to send a first request to get the record, and a second to resolve .HTTPS records are still too new for this use case. Back to the drawing board! 📐As a compromise, the script returns the two nearest servers if they are at a similar distance from the user. Otherwise, it returns only the nearest one with a lower of 2 minutes.We can check it with . From Chicago, we get only the Ashburn server with a of 2 minutes, while from Mexico, we get both Ashburn and San Jose.doggo--gp-fromAvincent.bernat.ch doggo--gp-fromAvincent.bernat.ch doggo--reverse.161.44.145.28.219.155 The complete code is a bit more complex. It works around RoutingEngine.getClosestServer() supporting only IPv4, and it handles the case where there are not enough alive servers to build an answer.Route 53 covered one additional use case of mine: serving to solve DNS-01 ACME challenges. Unlike Route 53, Bunny DNS cannot restrict access to a single zone with a fine-grained access policy. As this usage requires neither high availability nor low latency, I replaced Route 53 with Hickory, a memory-safe DNS server written in Rust. It supports automatic DNSSEC signatures and dynamic updates. Its configuration is simple:The provided zone file only seeds the database on first start. I delegate DNS-01 challenges to this zone with records:Unfortunately, Bunny DNS cannot publish a record in a zone. I need one to secure the zone and certificate delivery. Therefore, I host the zone on deSEC, a free DNS hosting service run by a non-profit organization based in Berlin. I derive the record to publish in from the record of :acme.luffy.cx dig@nsupdate.luffy.cxDNSKEY+noall+answerdnssec-dsfromkey-aSHA-256-f-Overall, I am quite happy with the switch to . There are still a few rough edges, like the inability to publish records, the lack of HTTP/3, and the IPv4-only RoutingEngine.getClosestServer() helper. The bill went from US$5 per month to US$1. So far, performance is on par with AWS, but I only finalized the current setup, including the server in Sydney, in late October. I need a bit more time to gather more data, and I'll post a short update. 📈

item.title: John Goerzen: Letter from a Kansan: “Would You Rather Be Right or Happy?”
item.author: John Goerzen
item.content:encoded: As a person that has lived in Kansas almost all my life, I have never seen such good political news for this state as we got this week. It is a stunning rebuke of fascism from across the country.One of the many pieces of wisdom from mechanic Tom Magliozzi is this question: “Would you rather be right, or happy?” He often asked it in the context of somebody that had just won an argument.This is my plea to all our progressive friends: remember that question, and keep it in mind carefully over the next 2 years. We can either build on this momentum for an even bigger victory in 2028, or we can start to lose this unique coalition.Kansans spend our lives being misunderstood and forgotten.Many of us, myself included, visit large cities regularly.It is a more surprising event when someone from a large city drives down one of our dirt roads. The kind of road that leaves your car covered in mud when you drive your daughter to school. The kind of road that we drive on for 3 miles before we reach the nearest paved road.Statisticians label Topeka, the capital of Kansas and city of 126,000 people, as rural.The nearst town to me, 7 miles away, has a population of 600. In winter, many people here still leave their keys in their running, unlocked cars while they run into the grocery store. The person at the bank, the owner of the grocery store, the mechanic, the electricians, the builders, the people that run the local museum, all know my name and recognize me. Not because I’m famous locally, but because this is normal here. We are a community, a real one.Yet I’ve lost long-time friends, especially from the west coast, because, while I’m progressive, I still talk to Republicans. They thought Republicans are so evil, they ought to be shunned and ostracized.It probably doesn’t compute to a San Franciscan what it means to live in a county that went 80% for Trump one time. A county of about 10,000 people living in a space larger than Los Angeles, New York, and San Jose — combined. (Those cities have a combined population of about 13 million, living on the same amount of land as 10,000 people do out here.)If I avoided talking to Republicans, it wouldn’t be them that would be isolated. It would be me.Out here, many of us have lived with each other for generations. We may go on living with them for generations. If somebody’s car is stuck in the mud, the first person that comes by with a truck and a rope will probably pull them out. Nobody asks who you voted for. This is what you do for neighbors, because neighbors are humans, and next time it might be me that’s stuck in the mud.I can be as incensed as anyone else about what the fascists are doing. I don’t have direct knowledge of how a lot of people vote. But I take a deep breath sometimes and remind myself: these are my neighbors. I’ve seen them go out of their way to be kind and generous with all walks of humanity. (Yes, even whatever groups you’re imaginging to argue with me about.)This is part of how Adam Hamilton defeated Roger Marshal. The anti-Trump sentiment wasn’t enough on its own. Lifelong Republicans dissatisfied with how Trump handled things weren’t just going to vote for any Democrat. They needed someone that was safe. Someone that talked to them as humans. Someone that respected them.Adam Hamilton went and shook hands with MAGA protestors at his events. He told them “I want to be your senator, too.”I have already been seeing some progressives say things like, “Don’t cut them any slack. Remember how many times people voted for fascism! They need to still be ostracized.”That, folks, is the way we lose. It is the wrong strategy everywhere. And it is especially culturally wrong in the close-knit communities — again, actual communities where people know each other and have for years — that make up the heartland.Building relationships with people different than us is our best chance to build on this coalition. And, isn’t that what progressive values call for?So, celebrate this victory. Clap for all the activists that made it happen.And, before you set off to alienate your new and tentative allies, ask yourself:“Would I rather be right? Or win again?”

item.title: Juan Manuel Méndez Rey: Hello, Planet Debian
item.author: Juan Manuel Méndez Rey
item.content:encoded: Hello, Planet Debian. My blog was added to the Planet today, so I think the polite thing is to introduce myself before you start finding my posts between yours.I am Juan Manuel Méndez Rey, from Sevilla. In Debian I am mendezr, and on OFTC I am Vejeta. I have been using Linux since 1994 and Debian since 1998. For a long time that was all: a happy user, installing, breaking things, reading the mailing lists from the outside. I started contributing in October 2025, and last month I became a Debian Maintainer.The way in was a friend. Back in 2019 Arturo Borrero Gonzalez filed RFP #943703 for Stremio, and for years he kept telling me I should pick it up. In September 2025 I finally listened and turned it into an ITP. It took longer than I like to admit, but Stremio is now in Debian, and I told that story here. A six year old RFP turned out to be a very good first package.Somewhere along the way I discovered that what I enjoy most is bringing old software back.The first one came from tille, who asked for help in #debian-tinytasks with xwpe, a Borland style programming editor for the terminal that nobody was looking after. I adopted it, and then I ended up as its upstream maintainer too. I fixed the old bugs and added LSP and DAP, so now an editor from 1993 can debug Go. It ships on several distributions, in Homebrew and on the BSDs. The canonical repo is on Codeberg, and the long version is in this post.The second one is older and took much longer. Conquer is a Unix strategy game written by Ed Barlow and Adam Bryant in 1987, and I lost many hours of my youth to it. It never had a free licence. I first asked about it on debian-legal in October 2006, and I spent the next 20 years tracking down the authors, one email at a time. Today Conquer v4 and V5 are GPL-3.0. It is not packaged in Debian yet, that is the next step, but you can already play it in the browser.CEF took me six months and brought me into the Chromium team, and these days I am mostly with the syft, trivy and grype security stack and with Scala 3 and sbt for Debian.To Arturo, for the nudge. To dilinger, tille and tsimonq2, my DM advocates, for trusting me.And if you can sponsor uploads for syft, trivy, grype or the Scala work, I would be very grateful. The details are on my wiki page.
